talks.title: Weaving Agentic AI into the SOC: A Practical Playbook for Operationalizing and Scaling Autonomy
talks.teaser: Weaving Agentic AI into the SOC: A Practical Playbook for Operationalizing and Scaling Autonomy.
talks.summary:
Overview: Benjamin Spencer of Optiv joins an ISMG session on weaving agentic AI into the SOC, sharing practical lessons from MDR operations and SOAR modernization efforts.

Key Topics: Where autonomous agents add measurable SOC value versus where they don't; guardrails for safe AI deployment; organizational hurdles from pilot to production; and avoiding treating AI as upgraded SOAR without engineering.

Technical Details: Spencer shares war stories from Optiv's attempt to operationalize agentic AI in detection and response workflows, emphasizing that AI agents require the same rigorous engineering as traditional SOAR playbooks, not less.

Takeaways: Agentic AI in SOCs needs deliberate engineering and guardrails, not just vendor promises. Teams should identify specific high-value triage tasks rather than attempting full autonomy replacement.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Benjamin Spencer, Product Director for Detection and Response Products at Optiv, joins ISMG's Tom Field to present an operational playbook for integrating Agentic AI into the modern Security Operations Center (SOC). Spencer details Optiv's real-world deployment of autonomous AI agents across managed detection and response (MDR) environments, achieving an 80% reduction in Mean Time to Respond (MTTR). The session addresses the critical architectural and cultural hurdles of moving from rigid SOAR playbooks to agentic autonomy, highlighting guardrails, structured outputs, and operational lessons learned.

Key Topics:
- The failure of traditional SOAR playbooks vs. the transition to autonomous Agentic AI
- Achieving an 80% reduction in Mean Time to Respond (MTTR) across enterprise MDR workflows
- War stories: mitigating token waste, alert mixing, and hallucinations via structured outputs
- Designing SOC workflows around AI autonomy with human-in-the-loop validation

Technical Details:
Spencer begins by contrasting Agentic AI with legacy Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms. While SOAR promised complete SOC automation, in practice it created brittle, rigid playbooks that failed whenever alert parameters deviated slightly from expected logic—a limitation Spencer compares to hooking an electric motor up to ancient factory pulleys. In contrast, Agentic AI leverages large language models to dynamically aggregate data, interpret alert context, and execute investigative steps across disparate telemetry sources. Across Optiv's live enterprise deployments, operationalizing autonomous agents delivered an 80% reduction in MTTR, accelerating triage and freeing security teams from repetitive tasks.

However, moving from pilot to production revealed significant technical pitfalls. Spencer shares early development "war stories," where Optiv initially attempted to treat LLMs as an advanced SOAR by dumping raw, unfiltered security alerts and telemetry directly into the context window. This naive approach resulted in massive financial expenditures on token consumption and produced unusable outputs: the model frequently hallucinated, mixed context across unrelated customer alerts, and generated nonsensical remediation guidance. To overcome this, Optiv completely re-engineered the architecture away from free-form prompt engineering toward deterministic constraints. The team implemented strict input curation, ensuring agents receive only the specific telemetry required for the alert type, and mandated structured JSON output schemas to prevent open-ended hallucinations.

Furthermore, Spencer emphasizes the necessity of human-in-the-loop guardrails. Because LLMs are inherently non-deterministic and can generate factually incorrect conclusions with extreme confidence, SOC workflows must require human analysts to perform sanity checks on agent-generated findings before executing disruptive response actions. Instead of attempting to bolt AI onto existing human analyst routines, successful organizations must redesign workflows around what agents do best—Tier 1 and Tier 2 alert enrichment, context aggregation, and reporting—enabling human analysts to supervise agent maturity.

Key Takeaways:
Integrating Agentic AI into the SOC requires rethinking security operations rather than retrofitting AI onto obsolete SOAR processes. Organizations must enforce strict guardrails, including structured output schemas and curated data ingestion, to prevent hallucinations and runaway token costs. Crucially, autonomous agents should handle data aggregation, triage, and summarization, while human analysts remain in the loop to sanity-check findings before executing response actions. This architectural paradigm saves dozens of analyst hours weekly, allowing security personnel to focus on higher-tier threat hunting and defensive maturity.

Webinar Scope and Audience

ISMG’s Tom Field hosts Optiv AI services co-lead Brian Goldenbeck and Cisco distinguished security architect Keith O’Brien for senior practitioners navigating AI security market challenges. The session targets data governance, privacy, enterprise-grade AI deployment, and client pain points across industries rushing AI products to market.

People and Process Challenges

Goldenbeck notes organizational change management, AI literacy, and employee fear often exceed technical difficulty. Successful programs need champions, training, and messaging that AI augments rather than replaces roles while addressing repetitive-task automation expectations from leadership.

Technical Security and Agent Governance

Keith O’Brien describes Cisco’s AI security focus, including classifier models in AI Defense products protecting LLM applications. On agentic AI, he recommends phased feedback loops—heavy human reinforcement while agents learn tasks, then reducing interaction once behavior stabilizes—plus controls on data access, user interaction, and when autonomous actions should be disabled.

talks.summary:
Cloud Hype Versus Reality

Optiv advisers Derek Nash and Ramy Hijazi discuss cloud transformation beyond early “lift-and-shift saves money” dreams. Gartner hype-cycle disillusionment gave way to nuanced understanding: cloud shifts economics, enables agility, and demands workload fit—not universal datacenter replacement.

Business Operating Model

Ramy frames cloud as the business operating model with security as the control plane (like traffic lights enabling speed). Value now comes from faster delivery, reorganized teams, and new revenue—not marginal infra savings after datacenter virtualization already captured efficiencies.

Misalignments to Fix

Common gaps include unclear migration rationale, DevOps shipping faster while security plays catch-up, and missing shared north-star metrics. Example: a healthcare client aligned on “digital company with personalized patient experiences” to unify IT, security, and business KPIs.

Security-as-Code Blueprint

Success requires embedding automated guardrails (policy-as-code) early, shared goals across functions, and treating secure transformation as continuous enablement rather than bolt-on review—especially after outages expose operational dependencies.

talks.title: Mastering Machine Identity with 47-Day Certificates
talks.teaser: Mastering Machine Identity with 47-Day Certificates.
talks.summary:
Shorter certificate lifetimes

Optiv's Patrick Dunaway and Palo Alto Networks' Florin Lazurca discuss public TLS lifetimes shrinking toward 47 days. Shorter validity reduces compromised-key exposure and forces validation, but sharply increases renewal frequency and velocity—especially with the first 200-day milestone approaching.

Why manual processes fail

Gartner-cited averages of hours per certificate multiply into thousands of hours annually for large estates, with workload doubling this year and rising toward 12x by 2029. Human delays, staff turnover, inconsistent handoffs, and misconfigurations already cause outages; faster cadence removes recovery buffer.

Operating model shift

Organizations must move from periodic, checklist-driven renewal to continuous discovery, policy enforcement, alerting, and orchestrated deployment across load balancers, APIs, firewalls, and hybrid multi-CA environments. Vendor-hosted certificates complicate automation when CLM tools and workflows are fragmented.

Solutions and crypto agility

Experts recommend visibility, early alerting, native integrations, high automation targets (~97%), and managed PKI services for scarce expertise. Crypto agility—rapid CA, algorithm, and key rotation—is essential for distrust events, SEC breach-notification rules, and post-quantum transitions as machine identities outpace human identities.

talks.title: FIFA: Securing the Game - Defend Against Cyber Threats Ahead of the 2026 World Cup
talks.teaser: Maps likely cyber threats to the 2026 World Cup and the preparation steps organisations can take beforehand.
talks.summary:
This Optiv webinar looks at the cyber risks tied to the 2026 FIFA World Cup, which will be spread across Canada, the United States and Mexico with 48 teams. The speakers argue that major sporting events have long attracted disruptive actors, and that the wider footprint creates many soft targets. Expected threats include denial-of-service attacks against venues and broadcasters, point-of-sale malware, ransomware, phishing and smishing that borrow event names, account takeovers on betting apps, deepfakes and rogue Wi-Fi. Sponsors, third parties, fleet vehicles and connected CCTV systems are also flagged as exposure points, and one case was described in which a hacker reportedly tracked a Department of Justice attorney by hacking his phone and nearby cameras.

Danny Pickkins frames "left of boom" as the preparation work done before malicious activity is detected. He suggests reviewing incident response plans and playbooks, confirming backups are immutable, rehearsing restoration and crisis communications, and confirming retainers with providers, legal counsel and cyber insurers. Tabletop exercises should test scenarios such as ransomware, insider threat, point-of-sale breach and outages, and should include executives so they can make decisions under pressure. Lena Dabbat adds that teams need clear roles, that exercises should run outside normal working hours because attacks often land at weekends or at night, and that police contacts for each jurisdiction should be identified in advance.

In the question round, the panel said drone threats are handled through airspace restrictions, jamming and law enforcement monitoring, and that only a small share of volunteer applicants are vetted. DDoS resilience was tied to layered defences, failover and cloud-based traffic distribution, with thresholds agreed in advance. The closing message was to practise, keep documentation current, look after staff during long shifts, and not assume a smaller organisation is out of scope.

talks.title: ’s James Turgal on NewsNation Discussing Potential Iranian Cyberattacks
talks.teaser: Outlines Iranian-linked cyber risks to critical infrastructure and everyday defensive practices for organizations and individuals.
talks.summary:
The segment frames growing worry about large-scale cyber activity tied to Iran, alongside ransomware and credential theft aimed at individuals and institutions. The guest describes Iran’s documented focus on government bodies, critical infrastructure, finance, and private companies, including website defacement, deepfake propaganda, and wiper malware. He highlights Cyber Avengers as a prolific Iranian-aligned group, citing nine water and water-treatment facility incidents across multiple U.S. states in 2023, and argues that healthcare, water, and food supplies remain especially alarming targets given real-world harm from past hospital disruptions.

The discussion turns to how attackers reach industrial control environments, using the 2023 cases as an example involving an Israeli supplier’s controllers and a zero-day that enabled backdoor access, followed by lateral movement, data theft, and ransomware or wipers. Credential harvesting, hardware and software backdoors, and long dwell time on compromised networks are emphasized as recurring patterns.

Viewers are urged toward cyber vigilance at home and work: strong authentication, regular password hygiene, knowing normal network behavior to spot spikes or mass exfiltration, vulnerability assessments, and timely patching amid heightened Iranian threat activity. AI-driven spear-phishing at scale, coordinated mass attacks, dark-web data sales, and adversary use of fake U.S. online personas—including remote IT job schemes—are raised as reasons to expect continued large-scale incidents rather than isolated one-off breaches.

talks.title: #OptivNews: James Turgal on CBS Chicago Discussing AI-Powered Tax Scams
talks.teaser: Explains how AI helps scammers run tax fraud and how to spot fake IRS contacts.
talks.summary:
Ahead of tax day, James Turgal, vice president of cyber risk and strategy at Optiv, speaks with a news host about how artificial intelligence has changed tax fraud. He describes a rise in AI-powered phishing and criminals using automation for tax fraud and identity theft. Stolen Social Security numbers, found or bought on the dark web, are used to file thousands of fraudulent tax returns and other forms such as W-9s.

He also points to threat actors who have built their own GPT-style tools, naming WormGPT and FraudGPT, to support their operations. The IRS has automated checks against this kind of fraud, but he stresses that a human reviewer has to stay in the loop as the final check.

For the public, the advice centres on how the IRS actually makes contact. The agency usually reaches people first by postal mail, and it sends texts or email only with a person's permission. An IRS agent will not demand payment by PayPal or gift cards, or threaten arrest or immigration consequences. Anyone with doubts should check the sender's address, since anything not coming from irs.gov is likely a scam. Suspicious messages can be verified on the IRS website and reported to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov.

talks.title: Take Control of Your Data: Privacy Settings in Your Favorite Apps
talks.teaser: Shows how to review app permissions, browser privacy settings and smart device data sharing to limit what gets collected.
talks.summary:
The panel covered how people can take control of their data by adjusting settings on the phones, apps and browsers they already use. Speakers recommended reviewing app permissions one at a time, since requests for microphone, camera, contacts or clipboard access often go beyond what an app needs. They also discussed privacy-focused browsers and global opt-out signals such as GPC, noting that some state laws expect businesses to honor them while enforcement of many of those laws has been stayed.

On connected devices, the panel described how thermostats, TVs, wearables and toys collect habits, location, occupancy and health data. A survey mentioned in the session found that only 14% of people check a manufacturer's privacy policy before buying, and 52% of homeowners with a smart thermostat did not know how its data was collected. Suggested steps included moving smart devices to a guest Wi-Fi network, turning off unneeded features, and asking whether data goes to third parties.

The webinar ended with how shared data feeds advertising, since search and social platforms fund free services by turning usage into interest profiles. The main takeaway was to read privacy notices before buying or installing, share deliberately, and favor privacy-focused vendors.

talks.title: #OptivNews: James Turgal Talks Latest U.S. Treasury Hack on FOX 2 San Francisco
talks.teaser: A security leader explains how AI amplifies ransomware and phishing while recent breaches highlight third-party vendor risk.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with reported denials and accusations around a breach of U.S. Treasury workstations, including access through a third-party software provider, alongside ongoing concern over the Salt Typhoon espionage campaign affecting telecommunications and private communications. The host frames 2024 as a record year for ransomware and asks how artificial intelligence is changing both hostage-style crime and broader intrusions.

The guest argues that machine learning lets ransomware operators move faster, target more organizations at scale, and map victim technology stacks to prioritize weaknesses. He describes criminal use of AI agents and branded fraudulent models on underground markets, and says AI can make phishing and deepfake content far more convincing and widespread.

On lessons from Treasury and telecom incidents, he stresses that major breaches increasingly ride third-party access and that China represents a top-tier nation-state threat. Practical takeaways for governments and large firms include inventorying vendors, demanding baseline security hygiene from partners, and maintaining resilient, actionable backups. He closes by noting defenders are adopting AI for predictive and behavioral analysis to find and close gaps more quickly.

talks.title: #OptivNews: Sean Tufts Discusses Holiday Cyberattack Surge on ABC7 Los Angeles
talks.teaser: A security expert explains holiday scam spikes, common phishing lures, and steps like credit locks and password managers.
talks.summary:
Holiday shopping and year-end workplace pressure create a predictable window when both employees and security teams are distracted, and attackers deliberately raise the volume of familiar scams during that period. The discussion frames the surge as more of the same phishing and invoice fraud, amplified by fake shipping notices, gift messages, and seasonal subscription offers, plus watering-hole style storefronts that mimic legitimate retailers.

Practical guidance centers on shopping only through known merchants, scrutinizing marketplace sellers even on major platforms, and comparing seller history, reviews, and sales volume before checkout. When someone suspects exposure, the recommended first responses are freezing credit with the major bureaus and adopting a password manager to strengthen and consolidate credentials instead of reusing weak secrets.

The segment closes by urging everyday situational awareness while browsing and purchasing, treating elevated holiday traffic as an operational reality rather than a new threat category.

talks.title: #OptivNews: James Turgal on NTD News Discussing Chinese Cyberespionage
talks.teaser: A former FBI official explains the suspected Chinese breach of US telecom networks and why call records are valuable.
talks.summary:
In this short news interview, James Turgal, a former executive assistant director at the FBI, responds to reports that executives from several telecom companies were summoned to the White House over suspected Chinese cyber espionage. He calls the matter a serious national security problem. He describes how attackers, which he links to Chinese state security or proxies and possibly reached through third parties, got into major carriers by abusing access paths originally built so law enforcement could reach certain telecom traffic.

He explains that much of the encrypted communication between devices stays protected, while some lower-level communications may be readable. He says the investigation into the scope of the breach is still ongoing, and that the ability to monitor calls or export data is the alarming part. Call log data alone can support fraud, and if intruders track who is calling whom, they can build profiles of political figures, police, or others for later exploitation.

Asked to compare the campaign with Volt Typhoon earlier this year, he notes that these government code names refer to different layers of activity. Volt Typhoon targets critical infrastructure, while Salt Typhoon targets communications. Combining the data from both can give attackers a bigger picture for later operations. He says agencies working with critical infrastructure operators are now closing the vulnerabilities involved.

talks.title: In the Know: 2025 Cyber Trends and Predictions
talks.teaser: Two practitioners forecast how AI, zero trust, OT exposure, and tooling sprawl will shape security priorities heading into 2025.
talks.summary:
The session frames late-year planning for 2025 security posture and budgets. From federal and commercial vantage points, the speakers expect continuity with recent years while social engineering, phishing, deepfakes, and a more corporatized ransomware-as-a-service model keep easing initial access. They tie rising AI and machine learning adoption to both defensive detection and response automation and to more polished offensive campaigns, while noting federal guidance such as secure AI development recommendations and ongoing skills-gap pressure on hiring.

On critical infrastructure, the discussion contrasts traditional utility hardening with post-Colonial targeting shifts toward multi-jurisdictional food, logistics, and airline victims, intelligence-focused activity reminiscent of Volt Typhoon, and kinetic-adjacent risks such as GPS disruption affecting grid timing. Zero trust is treated as a practical standard—not only a buzzword—including OMB implementation expectations, identity and access basics, third-party access limits, and micro-segmentation challenges in OT and IoT. AI governance is emphasized over picking a single large language model: crown-jewel data handling, cautious adoption compared with early cloud mistakes, and pragmatic controls as legacy OT environments modernize.

Closing guidance stresses fundamentals alongside forward-looking bets: annual firewall hygiene, integrated security stacks that serve SOC analysts, tech rationalization when organizations run dozens of overlapping tools, and board conversations framed as strategic direction on AI and zero trust rather than acronym shopping. Audience questions extend the thread to cloud trust, EDR versus XDR overlap, and AI-enabled vishing across new channels.

talks.title: How to Secure AI
talks.teaser: Optiv speakers outline AI guardrails across literacy, strategy, risk, governance and application security.
talks.summary:
This Optiv video walks through five areas of securing AI: education and literacy, strategy, risk, governance, and application security. Host Jeremy Jones frames the question of whether organizations are adapting quickly enough and whether they understand the guardrails. Tiffany Shogren suggests teaching AI literacy by tying it to existing awareness topics such as data protection, ethical data use, and threat actor risks.

Randy Lariar says generative AI is starting to affect knowledge work, prompting organizations to rethink their business processes. Brian Golumbeck describes guardrails that begin with principles, an acceptable use policy, and standards, all under leadership governance. Network controls such as CASB or SASE DLP at the network edge can inspect AI interactions and detect or block risky use. Jennifer Mahoney notes that AI governance is still catching up and recommends layering it onto existing data and security processes using the NIST AI risk management framework, one piece at a time.

In the application security segment, Lariar explains that AI is now embedded in many applications and that generative AI lowers the barrier to writing code, changing how teams think about software. The main takeaway is that securing AI means building on current programs rather than starting from scratch.

talks.title: Breaking Down Barriers: DevSecOps & CSPM
talks.teaser: A panel explores multicloud visibility gaps, CNAPP versus CSPM, and how DevSecOps tooling bridges security and development teams.
talks.summary:
Enterprises rushed into multicloud and hybrid footprints, often ahead of mature cloud security practices. Panelists describe recurring pain: unknown cloud assets, shadow accounts, fragmented ownership between security and SOC, and alert noise from traditional tools that were built for static on-premises perimeters. They argue that inventory and relationship-aware visibility must come first, because misconfiguration—not the cloud itself—drives most critical risk.

The discussion contrasts cloud security posture management with the broader cloud-native application protection platform model. CSPM focuses on policy and configuration across providers; CNAPP bundles posture, entitlements, workload protection, data posture, API coverage, and pipeline integration. They emphasize reducing signal sprawl by preferring unified platforms that correlate exposures, permissions, sensitive data, and runtime issues rather than stacking point products.

Practitioners are urged to treat cloud security as people, process, and technology together: define operating models, democratize remediation views for developers and responders, embed guardrails in CI/CD, and operationalize tools after deployment. A staged maturity path—discover assets, prioritize business-critical findings, harden data and code paths, and respond in real time with traceable root cause—frames how advisory and platform partners aim to accelerate secure cloud adoption.

talks.title: + ClearShark's Jessica Hetrick Discusses New White House Guidelines on AI
talks.teaser: Explains how a new presidential AI directive shapes government safeguards, competitiveness, and protection of the chips behind AI.
talks.summary:
In this interview, Jessica Hetrick, speaking for Optiv and ClearShark, discusses a recent presidential directive on artificial intelligence and national security. She describes AI as technology that lets machines learn from data and perform tasks resembling human abilities. The guidelines, she says, push agencies to use AI to stay competitive with rival nations and to build governance with allied partners.

She warns that the bigger danger is missing chances to build new capabilities in logistics, planning, offense and defense, operations and analysis. Adversaries can misuse the same technology, so she urges AI literacy across organizations. On safeguards, she recommends ethical usage rules and compliance definitions for each agency, keeping confidential data out of AI tools, and balancing transparency with confidentiality through masking, redaction, shuffling and name replacement. She also points to vetting technology providers, guarding against insider misconduct, and testing AI systems regularly for weak points.

The closing part covers the directive's call to secure the advanced computer chips that power AI and to protect the inventions developers create. Hetrick ties this to supply chain risk management and cites CMMC as a sign of growing compliance pressure. She expects protections for AI-related technology to keep expanding as the technology evolves.

talks.title: Is Your Organization Ready for the Next Wave of Endpoint Security Modernization?
talks.teaser: A panel explores iterative endpoint modernization, AI-enabled threats, and unified platforms that tighten visibility and response speed.
talks.summary:
Rapid AI adoption is reshaping both attacker tradecraft and endpoint technology itself, from more convincing phishing to new on-device and cloud-integrated assistants that can expand data exposure. The discussion frames endpoint security modernization as an ongoing journey rather than a one-time project, especially for distributed workforces, legacy gear, and mixed operating environments.

Threat reporting cited in the session highlights adversary speed and evasion: average breakout time around 62 minutes, with the fastest cases under three minutes; roughly 75% of observed attacks are malware-free, which strains signature-centric prevention; and about 90% of successful intrusions still begin on endpoints. Speakers map common blockers—outdated prevention models, weak automation at fleet scale, fragmented tools, and visibility blind spots—and argue for consolidating on a cloud-native platform with EDR/XDR, integrated intelligence, and AI woven into analyst workflows rather than bolted on as a buzzword.

Optiv describes an advise-deploy-mature path for implementations, migrations, and maturing controls when teams lack staff or process depth. CrowdStrike emphasizes a single lightweight agent expanding to additional use cases over time, Charlotte AI grounded in platform data with auditable answers, and collaborative incident investigation tooling. Audience Q&A addresses realistic visibility limits, protecting endpoints outside direct control, reducing agent sprawl, hallucination risks via scoped data, and the skills analysts need to work effectively with AI copilots.

talks.title: #OptivNews: Optiv + ClearShark's Jessica Hetrick Talks Deepfakes Amid Elections
talks.teaser: Details election deepfakes, generative AI abuse, disinformation scale, trust erosion, and detection plus skepticism to spot synthetic fraud.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with election-season anxiety around synthetic media, including celebrity endorsement hoaxes and earlier robocall incidents, framing generative AI as a dual-use force that scales both legitimate capability and abuse.

The guest describes how automation helps adversaries flood the web with mimicked articles, fake personas, misleading sites, lifelike deepfake video, and synthetic audio. Examples cited span domestic primaries and elections abroad, often linked to conspiracy narratives or gaps in public knowledge. She argues the old assumption—that identifiable authors stand behind published material—is weakening, which erodes trust and makes satire, fakery, and fraud harder to separate.

Closing themes emphasize preparedness: governments worldwide debate policy guardrails for political use of AI, while defenders can apply machine learning to detection and monitoring. For practitioners and the public alike, the takeaway is disciplined skepticism—checking whether content provokes emotion, seems exaggerated or click-driven, carries suspicious links, or accelerates a narrative without corroboration.

talks.title: The World of Optiv MDR
talks.teaser: Describes a managed detection and response program that eases SecOps load, integrates security tools, and adds 24/7 analyst coverage.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing common security operations pain points: sprawling tools, weak processes, and teams that lack capacity to adopt newer capabilities. The speaker positions managed detection and response as a way to meet organizations wherever they sit on a maturity curve rather than forcing a full rip-and-replace overhaul.

The middle of the talk walks through what the service is meant to include end to end, from log ingestion and processing through detection, storage, and response, plus ongoing expert guidance. Flexibility with existing or preferred vendor technology is emphasized, along with optional automation such as SOAR workflows and AI-assisted log search, whether or not the customer already runs an in-house SOC.

The close stresses continuous coverage through globally staffed delivery centers operating around the clock, staffed by certified engineers and analysts. Outcomes mentioned span perimeter controls, security service edge, threat hunting, and incident detection and response, framed as one path among broader managed security offerings rather than a deep technical walkthrough.

talks.title: MDR in Action: Rapid Malware Response
talks.teaser: Walks through a managed detection case where a Mimikatz alert leads to host isolation and a disabled user account.
talks.summary:
This vendor demo follows a managed detection and response case that begins on an employee laptop compromised without the user's knowledge. An attacker tries to deploy Mimikatz, dump credentials from LSASS and move data out of the environment. The analyst's dashboard shows an AI-generated case summary, and SentinelOne had detected the Mimikatz file without mitigating it, so it remained live.

The analyst pivots through the case. The user's profile shows an accounts receivable role, which makes PowerShell activity against LSASS look out of place. Palo Alto network logs show an outbound connection to an address resolving to GitHub, which at least one VirusTotal engine flags as malicious. A script hash first seen two hours earlier is flagged by many more engines, and related detections point to earlier compromise. The analyst then runs a playbook that confirms client authorization in the ITSM system, isolates the host and removes the malware.

To close the case, the analyst disables the user's Active Directory account and forces a password reset, since LSASS access raised concern about the account itself. After the endpoint is cleaned, the account is re-enabled and the host reconnected, and the case is documented as a malicious external attack with the client's security team informed. The demo shows how a managed service pairs automated playbooks with analyst judgement for nonstandard cases.

talks.title: Three Things to Know to Rightsize Your Cybersecurity Tool Stack:
talks.teaser: Explains how to rationalize overlapping security tools through business alignment, control-centric planning, and ongoing maintenance.
talks.summary:
The speakers frame post-pandemic security spending as a sprawl problem: one-off products, hard integrations, and heavy administration now clash with tighter budgets and higher expectations. They argue technology rationalization should be continuous—woven into tool reviews and multi-year roadmaps—not a single checklist exercise.

Three implementation themes anchor the discussion. First, alignment with business outcomes and clear drivers (visibility, M&A, cost pressure) so teams ask the right questions. Discovery often surfaces unknown tools, weak asset management, and siloed buying; success requires cross-functional participation and skepticism toward assumptions, while treating some redundancies as intentional. Second, start from required security controls rather than vendor lists: map gaps, unwanted overlaps, and integration opportunities, then prioritize via risk—sometimes enabling existing features beats new purchases. Case studies cite shortened cloud migration planning and budget-cycle inventories yielding redundancies, needs, and integration targets. Third, sustain the program via roadmaps, broad business involvement, and data flows that make telemetry actionable—including closing loops into incident workflows.

Practitioners should identify objectives, assemble SMEs, define use cases and control coverage, assess tool maturity, and maintain rationalization as an operating habit.

talks.title: Build Resilience
talks.teaser: Connects executive leadership, critical assets, recovery culture, and industry awareness to rapid recovery after major cyber incidents.
talks.summary:
The segment defines cyber resilience as the ability to rebound quickly after adversity, with emphasis on large cyber incidents alongside disaster recovery needs arising from natural events, human error, or other catastrophes. It argues that mature security programs depend on executive leadership driving awareness training, supporting annual cyber awareness activities, and understanding security roles and responsibilities.

For security leaders, three priorities frame resilient programs: knowing critical assets and protecting data, fostering a staff culture oriented toward fast and efficient recovery operations, and staying current on industry trends while encouraging in-house innovation. Those themes tie operational readiness to sustained attention on what matters most when incidents strike.

The closing portion describes how a security services provider can align strategy with executives, support security operations and incident teams through tabletop and preparatory work, and supply technology partnerships aimed at modernization. It closes by treating cyber risk as business risk and favoring outcome-centered security goals.

talks.title: Less Pain, More Gain: Cybersecurity Awareness Month, 20 Years Later
talks.teaser: A panel explores how passwordless adoption, MFA, patching, and concise awareness training have evolved over two decades.
talks.summary:
Optiv hosts a Cybersecurity Awareness Month LinkedIn Live marking twenty years of the campaign. The conversation opens on resilience despite a tougher threat landscape, then walks through everyday controls with research from a six-thousand-person survey and organizational experience.

Passwords are treated as a failed default: reuse remains common, password-manager trust dipped after headline incidents, and both guests push MFA and passwordless paths that reduce friction. Software updates are framed as ongoing hygiene at work and at home, including routers and consumer apps, with patching linked to real breach lessons. Awareness messaging is shifting away from hoodie clichés toward short, useful touchpoints; generational survey gaps show Gen Z clicking more while doubting personal agency, whereas older adults face higher fraud losses. On generative AI, enterprise leaders weigh enablement against data loss via labeling, DLP, and blocking unsanctioned tools, alongside tightening privacy regulation.

The close returns to four practical behaviors aligned with CISA—MFA, strong unique passwords, phishing caution, and updates—and argues that doing basics well keeps most people and organizations in solid shape while the industry slowly matures.

talks.title: Ensure Compliance
talks.teaser: Coverage of Ensure Compliance from the conference program.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, an Optiv representative discusses what it means to ensure compliance from a cybersecurity perspective. Rather than treating compliance as a traditional, check-the-box exercise, organizations are urged to embed compliance as a non-static element integrated into daily activities and company culture.

### Key Topics
- **Moving Beyond 'Check the Box':** Modern cyber compliance requires shifting away from static compliance routines to continuous cultural integration.
- **Policy Over-Reliance Red Flag:** A primary pitfall for organizations is leaning too heavily on written policies and procedures without implementing independent assurance or validation to confirm controls are actually working.
- **Three Pillars to Ensure Compliance:**
  1. *Compliance vs. Security:* Recognizing that being compliant does not equal security, and maintaining the best security program does not guarantee compliance.
  2. *Regulatory Applicability:* Evaluating laws, regulations, and frameworks to understand which specific requirements actually apply to current business processes, as not every framework is relevant.
  3. *Foundational Integration:* Embedding compliance directly into daily operational activities to cultivate a naturally secure culture.

### Technical Details & Industry Practices
- **Validation and Control Assurance:** Although establishing foundational policies and procedures is essential, lack of active validation leaves unanticipated security gaps across the environment.
- **Optiv Services and Enablement:** The speaker highlights Optiv's approach to navigating complex regulatory landscapes through technology deployment aligned with regulatory requirements, advisory services provided by experienced practitioners, and partner network solutions.
- **Qualitative Compliance Metrics:** While quantitative data is commonly sought, valuable indicators of a mature compliance program are often qualitative. Specifically, a lack of an uptick in internal audit inquiries or regulatory investigations serves as a strong signal that compliance is successfully integrated.

### Takeaways
- Security and compliance must be treated as related but distinct disciplines.
- Do not assume policies equate to protection; validate implementation to eliminate unseen gaps.
- Embedding compliance into everyday business functions minimizes regulatory inquiries and builds sustainable organizational resilience. Note: The short transcript focuses on high-level operational strategy and does not introduce specific technical tooling or CVE details.

talks.title: Cybersecurity and Space: Protecting Communications, Research and Beyond
talks.teaser: Explores how jamming, VPN flaws, and legacy firmware threaten satellite networks and what defenders should prioritize.
talks.summary:
The session frames space systems as everyday critical infrastructure: weather, navigation, missile warning, and telecommunications, then walks through how conflicts such as the war in Ukraine extend into jamming, spoofing, and disruption of communications and utilities. A retired military intelligence leader ties those effects to strategic concepts like projecting power, information dominance, and situational awareness across air, land, sea, space, and cyber domains, including policy friction between national authorities and operators.

An incident response specialist dissects the Viasat campaign as a real-world case where attackers abused a misconfigured VPN appliance to reach management networks and break links between terrestrial modems and satellites, noting comparatively simple recovery via factory resets and hardware swaps while warning the field is still immature. The conversation covers why satellites cannot be truly air-gapped, supply-chain risk for launch vehicles and long development cycles, legacy fleets with weak firmware, Hack-A-Sat’s Project Moonlighter as proactive testing, and ground-station物理与人员 controls. They also debate satellite blackouts affecting elections or navigation, Silent Barker–style space monitoring, and when cyber attacks might be treated as acts of war.

Practitioners hear recurring defensive themes: encryption end to end, secure development before launch, defense in depth, executive buy-in, anomaly detection for long-dwell intrusions, public–private coordination, and borrowing lessons from cloud and remote workforce security—because orbiting assets are remote computers with decades-long lifetimes.

talks.title: Finding Opportunities Through Technology Rationalization
talks.teaser: Examines why security technology rationalization matters now and how leaders gain ROI from consolidation and gap analysis.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens on why rationalization has surged: years of rapid security innovation left many enterprises with overlapping tools, while higher capital costs and investor scrutiny force harder choices about what truly serves the business. Panelists tie that trend to crowded vendor markets and the shift from adding niche products toward integrated platforms and clearer return on existing spend.

The middle of the conversation centers on practical methodology. Security leaders are urged to map real use cases, run gap analysis application by application, and apply crawl-walk-run adoption so licenses and features match maturity and roadmap timing. Examples include using only part of an email security platform while other modules remain available, underusing bundled suites such as Microsoft E5, and integrating alerts into operational workflows. Staffing shortages reinforce the need for fewer dashboards, better vendor integration, and trade-offs between tool spend and headcount.

Closing themes treat rationalization as an ongoing discipline, not a one-time budget cut. Recommendations cover three-year roadmaps, early renewal assessments, testing in realistic environments, preserving training and professional services, partnering with IT finance legal and product teams, transparent decision processes aligned to organizational “true north,” and involving practitioners—not only executives—so consolidation strengthens posture and business enablement rather than simply removing capabilities.

talks.title: Are You SEC Ready? What You Need to Know
talks.teaser: Are You SEC Ready? What You Need to Know.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this LinkedIn Live flash panel hosted by Optiv, Managing Partner Justin Williams, Vice President of Cyber Risk Strategy and Board Relations James Turgal, and Director of Strategy and Risk Management Adam Wisnieski analyze the SEC's newly adopted cybersecurity disclosure rules finalized on July 26. The panel breaks down what the finalized regulation requires for public companies, boards of directors, C-level executives, and third-party risk management under aggressive compliance timelines.

### Key Topics
- **Regulatory Timeline and Deadlines**: Following official publication in the Federal Register, incident reporting under Form 8-K / Item 1.05 requires compliance 90 days post-publication (marking December 18 at the latest). Annual disclosure rules (Item 106) take effect for annual 10-K filings for fiscal years ending on or after December 15, 2023 (such as calendar-year filers on December 31). Smaller reporting companies are granted an extended window of 180 to 270 days.
- **Materiality and Four-Day Disclosure Window**: The rule requires public companies to disclose a material cybersecurity incident on Form 8-K within four business days after determining materiality. Determining materiality depends on the perspective of a "reasonable investor," evaluating qualitative and quantitative impacts such as financial conditions, operational results, data loss, vendor relationships, and brand impact.
- **Management and Board Governance (Item 106)**: Registrants must describe their processes for identifying, assessing, and managing material cybersecurity risks, as well as management’s role (specific positions or committees) and board oversight. The panel notes that while specific cybersecurity board qualifications were not mandated, significant accountability and oversight pressure are placed squarely on CISOs and CEOs.
- **Supply Chain and Third-Party Risk**: Third-party service provider compromises affecting a registrant are not exempt; material impacts originating from vendors must still be reported, potentially resulting in dual filings if both entities are registrants. Companies are also expected to disclose their reliance on external cybersecurity service providers.
- **National Security and Law Enforcement Exceptions**: Unlike earlier proposals, the final rule provides a safe harbor allowing the U.S. Attorney General to delay public disclosure for 30 days due to national security or law enforcement risks, extendable to 60 days, and up to roughly 120 days in extraordinary circumstances.

### Technical Details
- **Item 1.05 (Form 8-K)**: Focuses on incident disclosure, requiring details on the nature, scope, timing, and material impact (or reasonably likely material impact) of an incident within four business days of a materiality determination.
- **Item 106 (Form 10-K)**: Mandates annual disclosures regarding risk assessment and management processes, prior incident impact, committee and management roles (including Item 106(c)(2)), prevention/mitigation monitoring, and reporting up to the board.
- **Materiality Determination Process**: The panel emphasizes that the four-day clock starts upon determining materiality, not at the moment of initial triage or discovery. However, companies cannot artificially delay investigations beyond reasonable timeframes established by standard operating baselines.

### Takeaways
Organizations have a narrow window (approximately 90 to 120 days) to establish cross-functional alignment. Compliance cannot remain an isolated security issue; it demands an integrated operating model across three main pillars: IT/cybersecurity, legal (General Counsel), and finance (CFO/accounting). Organizations must explicitly document their incident triage and value stream mapping to define quantifiable harm and determine precisely who makes the materiality determination and briefs the board.

talks.title: Build an Incident Response Playbook with Cyber Threat Intelligence
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss how threat intelligence can enrich incident response playbooks, risk decisions, and purple team exercises.
talks.summary:
This live panel from Optiv's threat management practice looks at how cyber threat intelligence can support incident response and offensive security work. The panelists begin by arguing that automated technical intelligence is most useful for enriching indicators and alerts, giving responders quick context that speeds triage. During an active incident, they say, responders need information that is timely, relevant and actionable, while deeper trend analysis belongs after the fact.

The conversation then turns to playbooks. The speakers suggest keeping the desired end state fixed while letting analysts adapt their steps, which they describe as uniformity of work with independence of analysis. They stress knowing normal business behavior first, since intelligence only adds value once a baseline exists, and they warn that too much data creates fog as much as too little. Risk was another theme: accepted risks should be documented, walled off into a segmented zone and watched with focused sensors. One offensive panelist described blending the profiles of known threat groups to build emulations tailored to a client's sector, with purple teaming as a way to turn those results into detection gains.

To close, the panelists noted that CTI takes time to pay off, and recommended trusted sources that avoid fear-driven content. They observed that attackers keep reusing methods that still work, so tracking historic tradecraft matters, and the gTIC team maintains a prioritized software list for patching and visibility.

talks.title: MXDR in Action: Phishing Detection and Response
talks.teaser: Shows how a managed detection service catches a phishing compromise, triages the alert, and isolates the affected host.
talks.summary:
This short vendor demonstration follows a phishing attack on a new HR employee at the NewMedist credit union, a client of Optiv's managed detection and response service. The employee receives an email posing as internal IT, asking him to install a security update. Running the attached file launches a command that downloads more code and gives the attacker remote control of the workstation. The attacker then collects details about the new host, such as running processes, network and system information, and other user profiles.

The demo then shows how the service responds. Related alerts are merged into one incident using criteria set by Optiv to reduce alert fatigue, and the indicators are enriched with threat intelligence. A SOC analyst triages the ticket, which already holds alert data pulled in through API integrations, and pivots into the analytics platform. Queries of Office 365 mail logs reveal the phishing subject and attachment, and Palo Alto logs show suspicious outbound connections to the malicious URL.

With the activity confirmed, the analyst isolates the host through the EDR's API without opening its console, and the isolation is confirmed within seconds. The user is told to contact IT support. The ticket is escalated to the client and stays open until both sides agree the activity is resolved, at which point the host can be released. The key takeaway is how correlation, enrichment and automated containment shorten the time from alert to containment.

talks.title: Rationalizing Data Investments
talks.teaser: Leaders explain how to justify security data spend, tame sprawl, and align detection investments with board and business priorities.
talks.summary:
The panel opens on how remote work, zero trust, and digital transformation have outpaced data plans, multiplying copies and third-party handling while budgets stay flat. Participants describe the tension between needing more telemetry for defense and losing track of where sensitive information lives when business units bypass overloaded IT.

The conversation shifts to governance and persuasion: inventory and lineage must stay current, stewards must own answers to what, where, how, and why data is collected, and security leaders should pair with revenue owners instead of pitching pure risk spend. Examples include reframing behavioral analytics as business insight, reusing tooling across marketing and security, tailoring ROI narratives to executive personalities, and turning prevented incidents into KPIs executives grasp.

They close on execution and privacy: milestone wins must show business outcomes, not just dashboards; funding needs honest communication when plans slip; and consumer rights to access and delete data challenge lakes and legacy apps. Cross-unit cooperation depends on culture, executive sponsors, and consistent storytelling when nothing has visibly “gone wrong.”

talks.title: CRS Case Study
talks.teaser: Explains a recovery framework that maps critical business systems and helps organizations restore operations after a cyber attack.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Optiv's Cyber Recovery Solution, a framework meant to reduce risk when a cyber attack hits. It is described as an extension of existing business continuity and recovery planning. The core idea is that an organization should know which systems matter most, have better detection on them, and be able to fully restore them after an adversary has attacked.

The speakers frame the problem as downtime: how quickly an organization can get running again and recover to a secure state, since systems can be compromised again if they are restored carelessly. They stress understanding the dependencies between systems, data and applications, and acting proactively before an incident. The solution starts by discovering and mapping critical business processes. One manufacturing example involved a customer ordering and delivery process that accounted for 97% of the organization's revenue. Mapping every system behind it allowed the company to add protection and detection and plan its recovery. A second client had a weaker sense of its business impact, so the team sorted processes into mission-critical revenue drivers, business-critical enterprise enablers, and supporting processes that improve efficiency.

The speakers close by pointing to their people, their products and their experience from large incidents, along with the ability to align with critical business capabilities and work across business leaders. The practical takeaway is to map business processes to the systems that support them first, then prioritize protection, detection and recovery around those processes.

talks.title: Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity: The Future of Big Data, Analytics, and Business.
talks.teaser: AI helps security teams spot patterns in big data, tie attack campaigns together, and speed containment when threats appear.
talks.summary:
The presentation casts artificial intelligence as a toolkit for organizing enormous, heterogeneous data flows. Sources include traditional databases, online and cloud environments, and internet-connected equipment from jet engines and turbines to household appliances. Those connections produce streams of information that attackers may prize, while consolidation, automation, and signal extraction make the same aggregates valuable for defense.

Security practitioners are portrayed as using AI to extend human judgment: always-on monitoring, recognition of patterns across volumes no individual or team could parse alone, and routing of the most meaningful anomalies to analysts. Investing in cyber programs alongside AI is said to stretch budgets and keep staff on higher-value tasks. Another scenario links isolated code fragments and log lines into wider attack campaigns, with cross-organizational sharing and machine-speed incorporation of comparable incidents strengthening posture. Properly configured alerts are said to clarify attack character faster and support quicker shutdown of compromised activity.

The talk stresses that processing speed, data scale, and maturing techniques make AI adoption practical now across industries for efficiency and growth. It closes by promoting next-generation AI and big data builds with security embedded from the outset so businesses can prioritize market success over cyber risk exposure.

talks.title: Nation States as Threat Actors | Optiv
talks.teaser: Former intelligence officers explain how nation-state actors pursue data and IP, and what boards should prioritize.
talks.summary:
James Turtle of Optiv and Nikki Brooks, a former intelligence officer, discuss nation-state threat actors and what they mean for clients. They compare the economic pressures on China and Russia, which they see as pushing both to seek new revenue. China is described as patient, focused on collecting personal data and advanced technology for the long term, while Russia is portrayed as more aggressive, using hackers for influence and disinformation campaigns.

The conversation then turns to smaller states such as Iran and North Korea, which the speakers see as opportunistic and often acting as proxies. Geopolitical relations, they argue, shape how active these actors are, and they note that stolen intellectual property lets adversaries close a technology gap cheaply. They also point to criminal tools such as Cobalt Strike being repurposed by attackers, and to deepfakes that could corrupt data as well as steal it.

For boards, the advice is to name the crown jewels in business terms, know where data sits and flows, and retire legacy systems and unneeded data. Overly strict lockdowns can stall innovation, and tools without context add noise, so security should be planned across each product's life cycle. The closing message is to think like an adversary and focus defences on what matters most.

talks.title: Managing Risk to the Research Enterprise
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss how universities can protect research from theft while keeping the openness that drives collaboration.
talks.summary:
This keynote panel, moderated by Justin Williams, looks at how academic institutions can manage risk to their research enterprise. The speakers frame the core tension: the openness, collaboration and reciprocity that make research effective also make it vulnerable to theft of intellectual property by state actors and others. They argue that protection should not limit openness, and that academia should lead the response in partnership with federal, state, local and industry partners.

Kevin Gamache describes a risk management framework developed with colleagues at the Hoover Institution. It has three steps: inventory processes, policies and technology solutions; apply operational security as a repeating cycle of identifying assets and threats, analyzing gaps and risks, and implementing countermeasures; and use a maturity model to grow a program from initial capability to full integration. David Petraeus links this to his military experience, describing risk assessment in four stages of planning, preparing, executing and assessing, with lessons fed back into tactics and procedures.

The panel closes by stressing risk awareness rather than risk aversion. The speakers warn that if universities do not act on their own solutions, legislation will be imposed on them, and they describe academic security as a team effort that needs federal and industry partners.

talks.title: Threat Trends Looking Forward | Optiv
talks.teaser: An enterprise security brief surveys ransomware monetization, supply chain targeting, purple teaming, and recent offensive research themes.
talks.summary:
The segment opens by framing today’s client risk around ransomware, describing actors who treat data theft as a business model and use hostage data to extort payment. It then shifts to what may come next, arguing that supply chain attacks will draw more attention after several high-profile incidents, and noting that some organizations already ask for simulations aimed at products and distribution paths to map attack chains into and through customer environments.

The middle ties that landscape to purple teaming: offensive work that models modern TTPs while pairing deliberately with defenders to harden posture. The speaker also describes a research publishing program that shares tester findings with clients, citing work on endpoint detection innovation, mobile device management links to email infrastructure for password-guessing scenarios, and abusing device authentication flows in Office 365 to support phishing.

It closes on how the organization positions services against current—not legacy—threats, emphasizing attack simulation paired with defensive planning as the environment changes. Practitioners should treat ransomware and supply chain compromise as sustained priorities, use collaborative red-and-blue exercises to validate controls, and watch published research on endpoint, mobile, and identity abuse paths as concrete examples of modern tradecraft to test for.

talks.title: How to Get Inside a Hacker's Mind
talks.teaser: Outlines emulated attack approaches, testing programs, and readiness gaps organizations face across people, process, and exposure.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames defensive improvement around thinking like an attacker. It opens by arguing that emulation of sophisticated adversary behavior can surface weaknesses and guide remediation across software, hardware, and user-facing environments, while stressing that unknown flaws remain attractive targets.

It structures advice around three recurring organizational failures. Human error dominates breach statistics, so the speaker advocates structured identification and ranking of vulnerabilities through assessments and ongoing penetration testing, chained scenarios that mirror real attacks, and social engineering exercises such as spearphishing, media drops, and tailgating. A second gap is weak incident readiness; the middle section urges mapping off-network and physical risks, reviewing cloud configurations, addressing insider scenarios, and using breach simulation that steps outside routine test patterns.

The closing problem is incomplete coverage of the attack surface, with most environments tested on only a fraction of exposure. The talk promotes broader attack-surface management, scheduled differential testing, remediation that goes beyond patching, and targeted reviews of nonstandard assets. Practitioners should treat the session as a checklist for balancing people-centric testing, response planning, and scalable visibility rather than a deep technical walkthrough.

talks.title: Data Fabric | Optiv
talks.teaser: A consultative methodology ties ingestion, analytics, and governance so organizations can operationalize security and IT data at scale.
talks.summary:
Organizations often struggle to turn scattered security and business data into consistent, actionable insight. Competing priorities, shifting markets, and a changing threat landscape make access, organization, and use of that data feel overwhelming without a deliberate architecture.

The presentation describes a data fabric approach as a programmatic, vendor-neutral bundle of technology and services aimed at a resilient management layer. It walks through landing heterogeneous sources in a data landing zone, feeding analytics sandboxes and visualization for day-to-day workflows, and embedding governance for compliance, quality, privacy, and security. The same stack is framed as a way to modernize IT and security operations centers while controlling cost and risk, including controlled paths for external data sharing.

Delivery is organized in three phases: advisory work produces a blueprint of pain points, drivers, tools, and a technology roadmap; deploy scales pilots into production by onboarding sources and tooling across sites; operate focuses on adoption, training, optional managed support, and extending use cases. Practitioners should view the talk as a high-level operating model for unifying data pipelines rather than a deep technical build guide.

talks.title: Insider Risk: Conversation | Optiv
talks.teaser: Practitioners learn how holistic insider risk programs unite HR, cyber, and culture beyond reactive monitoring.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing insider risk as widely misunderstood: threats include malicious insiders, careless staff, planted accomplices, and nation-state recruitment of disgruntled employees—not a narrow “bad employee” problem. A former federal insider-program builder describes how siloed security, IT, and insider-threat teams doomed early efforts, and why success requires organization-wide strategy.

The discussion stresses a proactive, person-centric model. Logical signals such as odd logins or bulk downloads gain meaning only with HR and business context—for example, resignation notices or privilege differences. Speakers warn that tool sprawl without governance can overwhelm endpoints and erode trust, while mature programs correlate weighted indicators, define risk tolerance, and pilot focused rollouts. Remote and hybrid work expands physical, privacy, and training gaps; communication must explain that programs protect employees as well as data.

Closing guidance ties critical-asset identification to monitoring choices, cross-functional governance, and leveraging existing security capabilities before new purchases. Takeaways emphasize cultural fit, balanced controls that avoid breeding new insider resentment, and leadership communication from frontline staff to the board so programs build trust rather than “big brother” surveillance.

talks.title: Source Zero Con: Apex Predators - Top Threat Actors and How they Operate
talks.teaser: Proofpoint telemetry and breach statistics show how elite criminal groups target people, credentials, and supply chains over CVEs.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames “apex predators” as the most impactful cybercriminal actors and argues that people—not exposed services—are now the main prey. Remote work and cloud apps widened that human perimeter, while indirect routes through suppliers and weak third parties often beat frontal attacks on hardened networks.

Using Proofpoint volume data, ransom negotiation insights, and recent Verizon DBIR findings, the speaker shows email-led compromise dominating at scale: credential phishing, modular downloaders feeding ransomware, BEC losses outweighing ransom, and techniques such as macros, PowerShell, and legacy Excel 4.0 macros. A staged flower-shop lure illustrates how many manual steps attackers chain before code runs. Actor charts rank financially motivated groups worldwide, note arrests and regional shifts, and contrast spray-and-pray volume with rarer state-linked activity.

A long section revisits the SolarWinds-related campaign across FireEye, Malwarebytes, Mimecast, and Microsoft, stressing that poisoned updates were only one entry among password spraying, OAuth abuse, phishing, and delegated identity quirks. Practitioners are urged to align effort with the 85% human/credential breach pattern: MFA, protocol hardening, monitoring federation and Graph API behavior, risky mail roles, and people-centric analytics that map who is attacked, who clicks, and who holds sensitive access.

talks.title: Your Password Policy Sucks...and We Can Prove It!
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers crack passwords with GPUs and wordlists, and what policy, MFA and vaulting changes actually stop them.
talks.summary:
Joshua Platz, a principal security consultant at Optiv, presents findings from a year of anonymized penetration test results. In those tests, about two thirds of the perimeter compromises came from weak or default passwords, ahead of web application flaws such as SQL and command injection, missing patches and file upload issues. Many clients still allowed eight characters or fewer, while only about 15 percent enforced passwords of 12 characters or more.

The talk traces how password cracking has changed since the 2012 LinkedIn breach, moving from CPU tools like John the Ripper and rainbow tables to GPUs, dedicated cracking servers and cloud GPU instances. Amazon GPU pricing dropped 78 percent between April 2015 and April 2017, so cost per attempt became the key limit. The estimated cost rises sharply with length: about 85 cents for passwords up to seven characters, about $80 for eight and $7,500 for nine. The speaker walks through wordlists combined with transformation rules in hashcat, brute force, and mask attacks that target common password formats.

The recommendations are a 12-character minimum with complexity and 90 to 120 day rotation, 20 characters for administrators, and separate accounts where legacy systems cannot enforce the main policy. Other steps include blacklisting predictable words, auditing cracked hashes from the directory, requiring MFA on every perimeter service, and vaulting privileged credentials behind random passwords. Training remains necessary, because users will still find ways to choose weak passwords.

talks.title: Chips In
talks.teaser: Outlines an employee volunteer program that links security staff with youth outreach on basic needs, safe spaces and education.
talks.summary:
Amber Peacher, a client operations specialist at Optiv, introduces the company's community engagement program, which she chairs. The program lets active employees connect with one another while serving their communities, with a focus on youth and a link to security. It rests on three pillars, and she starts with basic needs: employee teams have collected hygiene kits for local nonprofits, volunteered at food banks, and run a virtual food drive that raised funds for over 400,000 meals.

The second pillar, secure communities, covers making spaces where children can thrive safer. Examples include painting playgrounds, cleaning up parks, and repairing affordable housing. She describes an urban garden that a local team built with a nonprofit at an elementary school in a district where about 85 percent of students qualified for free or reduced lunch. The garden supplied fresh produce to students during the school day, and children took part in the harvest and the replanting.

The third pillar uses skill-based volunteering to secure education through technology. Employees sit on panels and run workshops for audiences from kindergarten through college, sharing their skills and hoping to spark interest in cybersecurity careers. She closes by saying the program has grown over recent years and will keep bringing staff together. For security professionals, the talk shows how employee volunteering can be tied to youth education and cybersecurity outreach.

talks.title: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) with WinAutomation Demo
talks.teaser: A WinAutomation demo runs labeled UI actions to log into Salesforce, file a CTO case, and save screenshots as proof.
talks.summary:
The presentation walks through how robotic process automation is structured in WinAutomation. The middle pane holds a main function made of labeled actions that run sequentially, much like a flow: opening pages, entering credentials, clicking controls, filling fields, capturing the screen, and closing the session.

The speaker runs the task live against static demo data. After sign-on, deliberate waits let the page render before the next step. The flow opens a new CTO case, sets fields such as due date, status, case owner, partner, and assigned resource, then saves so a new record appears in Salesforce. The scenario mirrors repetitive day-to-day case logging; the inputs need not stay fixed for real use.

talks.summary:
Optiv and Varonis present a webinar on securing human-generated data, such as documents, spreadsheets, and recordings, in the setting of the Army's data plan. The speakers argue that organizations often cannot say who can reach their sensitive data, and that discovering the data and its access should come before protecting individual systems. They frame this as an inside-out approach to zero trust.

The middle of the session covers risk in Microsoft 365 collaboration. Creating one Teams team also creates a hidden mailbox, Azure Active Directory groups and SharePoint sites, and files shared through chat are linked from personal OneDrive, so access is spread across several consoles. One customer case involved a DoD team spending over forty thousand dollars a week cleaning up spills, and another involved a compromised account caught through geolocation alerts. The presenters showed dashboards of externally and publicly shared files and stale data, and described enrichment that adds user context and behavioral baselines to file activity, plus automated replacement of broad groups with least-privilege groups after a chosen analysis period.

To close, the presenters said that normalizing and enriching events can cut the volume sent to a SIEM, and that an incident response team can shorten investigations from about twelve hours to one and a half hours, citing a Forrester study. Practitioners should take away the need to find sensitive data, map who can access it, monitor that access continuously, and automate least-privilege cleanup.

talks.title: Is Cybersecurity Virus Resistant?
talks.teaser: Executives discuss how remote work during the pandemic reshaped security risk and the cyber investment market.
talks.summary:
The panel, drawn from Momentum Cyber, Night Dragon and Optiv, looks at how the sudden move to remote work during the COVID-19 pandemic changed enterprise security. The speakers describe a first triage phase in which companies rushed to connect staff. Traffic figures shared in the discussion show remote share rising from about 10% on weekdays and 20% on weekends before the outbreak to over 75 to 80% in the United States and Europe.

The middle of the discussion covers what companies bought and what they missed. Spending centred on VPNs, multi-factor authentication, anti-phishing email security and cloud access tools. The speakers warned about exposed remote desktop, citing about 1.4 million new RDP devices appearing on the internet in three months. They also flagged unmanaged personal devices and home routers, data leaking through file-sharing services, and nation-state actors who could persist through remote access without using zero-day exploits. Monitoring tools tuned to office behaviour were expected to struggle with the new traffic patterns.

Looking ahead, the panel framed a second phase focused on hardening the expanded attack surface, revisiting identity, insider threat and third-party risk, and a third phase of settling into a new normal. Managed security services and virtual security operations were expected to grow. On capital markets, cyber stocks were seen as resilient, private investors were expected to favour later-stage deals, and consolidation was likely. The closing message was that security is becoming more relevant and that leaders should plan long-term strategy now.

talks.title: Palo Alto Networks TechTip: Using the BPA to Talk About Cortex
talks.teaser: Shows how BPA and SLR results support Cortex XDR conversations on investigation causality and elastic logging through the data lake.
talks.summary:
The session outlines how partner architects use Best Practice Assessment and Security Lifecycle Review output to open customer discussions about Cortex XDR. Lifecycle review findings can surface spyware, command-and-control traffic, FTP, and other file-exchange patterns. Those items become prompts about how the organization would investigate today and whether analysts can see full event context and causality without piecing data together by hand.

The middle of the talk contrasts fragmented workflows—endpoint management, firewall logs, and other consoles—with Cortex XDR when Traps, Palo Alto firewalls, and telemetry feed the Cortex Data Lake. An example chain runs from Outlook through Chrome, an Excel file, and a PowerShell macro to illustrate reduced mean time to causality. On the assessment side, logging adoption leads into scaling: forwarding logs through the data lake instead of adding collectors, racks, and power, then using that store for XDR analysis. The presenter also notes Traps licenses used for visibility-only forwarding when another endpoint product handles prevention, and ideal customers already running Panorama and WildFire.

The close positions XDR as an extension of an existing Palo Alto deployment and points interested viewers to Optiv contacts for follow-up.

talks.title: The Shifting IAM Paradigm: It's Time for CISOs to Embrace IAM and Think Outside the Box
talks.teaser: A CISO panel makes the case for identity and access management, covering partner access, MFA and single sign-on.
talks.summary:
Organisations have invested heavily in cloud, network, endpoint and data protection tools, yet the panelists note that identity rarely appears among the risks chief information security officers name. Breaches depend on misused credentials, and access was long treated as an administrative task passed between help desk, HR and IT. As cloud, SaaS and mobile use grew, identity became a baseline that can be applied across applications, devices and users.

External identities such as partners, suppliers and resellers came up repeatedly. In one audit described, about 37 or 38 people were found using a single shared account whose owner had left years earlier. The panel favoured letting partners authenticate through their own directories with federated single sign-on, so the enterprise never issues them credentials. Regulators are also demanding fast, accurate answers about who holds access. On passwords, the goal is to add multi-factor authentication through smartphones, paired with single sign-on.

The advice for CISOs was to treat access as the keystone of the security program rather than a burden, and to begin by taking ownership of authentication for SaaS applications so controls such as endpoint checks apply before access is granted. Starting with an inventory of existing technology that carries identity context was also suggested. The takeaway is that knowing who holds access makes other controls work better and costs less than cleaning up after a credential-based breach.
