talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Palo Alto Tech Tip edition, Tony Tanzi, a partner architect for Optiv focusing on Palo Alto Networks, introduces GlobalProtect Cloud Service (GlobalProtect as a service). The offering is designed to help organizations manage GlobalProtect deployments across distributed environments, specifically addressing the security and operational challenges associated with supporting both remote networks and mobile users.

### Key Topics
- **Distributed Workforce and Security Challenges**: Organizations face difficulties maintaining consistent security policies across headquarters, remote branches, and mobile users. Traditional solutions such as traffic backhauling or hair-pinning lead to high costs and poor performance. In contrast, deploying disconnected point products at remote sites results in inconsistent security posture and operational overhead, while mobile users frequently bypass protections entirely.
- **GlobalProtect Cloud Service Solutions**: The service delivers unified policy enforcement across devices and locations without requiring complex on-premises hardware footprints at branch sites.
- **Shared Ownership Model**: Palo Alto Networks handles the underlying cloud infrastructure (ensuring availability, scalability, and reliability), while the customer retains control over policy creation, authentication, and log analysis.
- **Centralized Management via Panorama**: Customers can manage the cloud service alongside their existing physical and virtual firewalls directly within Panorama, reusing established configuration objects and policies.

### Technical Details
- **Mobile User Connectivity**: Connects endpoints using the GlobalProtect app installed on user devices, ensuring consistent corporate threat protection and access policies regardless of user location.
- **Remote Network Connectivity**: Remote branch networks connect to GlobalProtect Cloud Service using standard IPSec VPN-capable devices or SD-WAN.
- **Integration and Threat Intelligence**: Leverages Panorama for centralized policy definition and integrates with tools such as AutoFocus for threat intelligence across the next-generation security platform.
- **Licensing Structures**:
  - *Remote Networks*: Licensed via an aggregated bandwidth pool divided among branch locations, with tiers ranging from 200 Mbps to over 10,000 Mbps.
  - *Mobile Users*: Licensed based on user count, offering tiers ranging from 200 users to more than 50,000 users.

### Takeaways
GlobalProtect Cloud Service eliminates the trade-off between performance penalties from backhauling and policy fragmentation from disparate point products. By offloading infrastructure operations to Palo Alto Networks while retaining policy control and object reuse in Panorama, organizations can achieve consistent security prevention across all endpoints and remote offices.

talks.title: Palo Alto Networks Tech Tips for the Endpoint
talks.teaser: Surveys Traps 4.1 and 4.1.1 endpoint releases, spanning anti-ransomware, DLL guards, Mac analysis, kernel APC, and ESM content updates.
talks.summary:
The session walks through endpoint protection additions in Palo Alto Networks Traps releases 4.1 and 4.1.1. On Windows, anti-ransomware monitoring targets encryption-style behavior so files are less likely to be held for ransom, with the module enabled by default on NTFS, FAT, and exFAT volumes. DLL file protection extends malware controls to block malicious library loading, combining local analysis with WildFire intelligence and optional DLL whitelists that merge across rules.

Local analysis on Mac compares unknown Mach-O binaries to known-malware traits and can label files malicious or benign while offline, pending a full WildFire verdict. Child-process rules use parent and child command-line context to allow or block execution; Palo Alto ships tuned defaults that administrators can clone and adjust in the endpoint security manager. Kernel APC protection focuses on the stage where shellcode would run, blocking access to unmapped memory after kernel injection. The management server can also push automated content updates to agents, with choices to preview, install immediately, or stay manual; policy changes reach agents on the next heartbeat.

Release 4.1.1 adds Traps support on macOS 10.13 and refines DLL protection with separate global and process-specific rule types. Practitioners gain a concise map of which controls ship enabled, where policies are managed, and how Mac and Windows coverage diverged in these builds.

This Black Hat panel looks at why connected devices have become a practical route into enterprise networks. The discussion starts from a Microsoft report, as described by the moderator, that claimed nation-state actors had reached 1,400 organizations through common devices such as VoIP phones, IP cameras and video recorders. The panelists agree that the intrusion mattered more than the device itself: attackers use these units as a relay into the rest of the network, and security teams often never see them during purchasing or planning.

The middle covers weak authentication, default passwords and flat networks, along with the need to inventory devices, segment them and bring security into procurement. Firmware integrity, secure hardware elements and the supply chain come up as ways to build in device identity, while the panelists are skeptical that blockchain is needed in most cases. They also point to new NIST guidance, with its comment period open until September, that calls for configuration management and device logging. Baselining normal device traffic can make unusual connections stand out. Regulated devices such as medical and industrial equipment complicate patching, and incident response for them is rarely practiced.

The closing takeaways are practical: build modern authentication into headless devices, write security into procurement requirements, know what is on the network, and run tabletop exercises for an incident. The panelists stress that even without solving every problem, organizations should check the basics now.

talks.title: Stop Living in the Past A New Approach to Application Security
talks.teaser: Stop Living in the Past A New Approach to Application Security.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Joseph Amon, Chief Innovation Officer at Veracode, argues that traditional application security approaches fundamentally fail to support modern DevOps practices, which demand multiple releases per day, continuous deployment, rapid feedback, and deep automation. Traditional security operates via intermediaries and conducts testing primarily at the end of the development lifecycle, creating unacceptable delays for DevOps teams. Additionally, peripheral security technologies (firewalls, WAFs, endpoint protection) treat applications as black boxes, lacking visibility into application logic and data flow.

## Key Challenges Identified
DevOps requirements include multiple daily releases, rapid cycle times measured in minutes to hours, continuous testing throughout the lifecycle, and collaboration between developers and security teams. Traditional application security creates a gap: developers cannot access security tools directly, requests take days to resolve, and testing happens too late in the cycle. When vulnerabilities are discovered at deployment time, developers must redesign and reprogram, delaying releases significantly.

## Criteria for Modern Application Security
Amon identifies four essential criteria:
1. **Transparency**: Security tools must not interfere with developers' primary objectives (functionality, quality, performance)
2. **Incremental approach**: Technology must test smallest code snippets continuously throughout the lifecycle, not just at deployment
3. **Rapid implementation**: Response times measured in seconds to minutes, not days or weeks
4. **Insight**: Deep visibility into application logic and data flow, moving beyond black-box analysis

## Emerging Technologies
**Developer SAST and Team SAST**: Modern variations of static application security testing integrated into IDEs and cloud services, enabling developers to test code increments as they write them with turnaround times of seconds to minutes, then progressively tested at build level.

**RASP (Runtime Application Self-Protection)**: An agent seamlessly instrumented into runtime environments (Java Virtual Machine, .NET CLR, PHP engines) that monitors application behavior, distinguishes benign from malicious activity, and stops attacks by preventing malicious instruction execution or sanitizing input. Transparent to developers and operating specialists, always running once installed.

**IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing)**: Uses RASP technology combined with attack inducers (DAST, embedded generators, or Quality Assurance scenarios) during testing phases, providing high accuracy with minimal human involvement and always-running continuous monitoring.

**SCA (Software Composition Analysis)**: Metadata-based repository of millions of third-party components that detects vulnerable open-source components in applications. Amon recommends combining with SAST for complete coverage, as SCA lacks insight into actual code usage patterns.

## Lifecycle Integration
Amon demonstrates how these technologies integrate across the complete lifecycle: Developer SAST for individual code increments, Team SAST for build-level testing, System SAST for complete application testing (typically within one hour), SCA for component vulnerability analysis, DAST or IAST for runtime testing, and RASP for production protection.

## Market Predictions (through 2020)
Amon projects cloud-based security services will exceed tool-based implementations due to better transparency and scalability; majority of DevOps-adopting enterprises will adopt developer static analysis; SAST will exceed DAST for DevOps use due to DAST's need for excessive crawling and attack generation; approximately 25% of DevOps enterprises will adopt IAST; and more than 40% of enterprises will adopt SCA.

## Recommendations
Start adoption with traditional, mature technologies (SAST, DAST, SCA), preferring cloud services over tools for transparency and scalability. Gradually evaluate and adopt emerging technologies (developer SAST, IAST, RASP) in parallel. Apply all technologies at appropriate lifecycle phases rather than replacing existing approaches. Consider shifting IT security spending from network security (currently dominant) toward application security, as network security lacks application-level visibility.

talks.title: Keeping Privileged Accounts Privileged Webinar
talks.teaser: Shows why privileged accounts drive breaches and how a managed privileged access service supports governance and monitoring.
talks.summary:
The webinar introduces a privileged access management service from Optiv, delivered with CyberArk tooling, and opens with the case for why privileged accounts sit at the center of breaches. The presenter cites rising breach counts, reports that most password-related breaches involve privileged credentials, and defines privileged accounts as administrator, domain admin, sudo and similar accounts that grant higher permissions. He groups threat actors into hostile insiders, users who push past their boundaries, and unwitting actors who expose credentials through careless practices.

He then outlines what a privileged access program needs: a working definition of privileged access for the organization, a documented governance framework, removal of excessive standing rights, and processes for onboarding new applications, mergers and shadow SaaS accounts, with continuous monitoring. He explains why these programs are hard to staff, citing round-the-clock monitoring, scarce trained people and the need for fast detection and response. The service components he describes include a technical project manager, release and change management, incident management, reporting and an onboarding path of about 30 days to full operation.

A healthcare case study describes a client with a partly deployed vault, a shortage of trained staff and exposed domain-level servers. After the provider extended the deployment to session recording, audit findings, and continuous monitoring, leadership gained confidence in its controls. The closing Q&A covers how privileged account definitions are shifting toward secrets in DevOps pipelines, cloud and automation, and how existing CyberArk customers would be onboarded.

talks.title: Webinar: Identity Your Wall or Weakest Link
talks.teaser: Explores why identity controls matter more than perimeter spending and how programs can shift from weakest link to strong wall.
talks.summary:
The session frames identity and access management as the center of a modern cybersecurity program, arguing that perimeter-focused spending leaves organizations exposed once attackers obtain a user context. A penetration-testing anecdote illustrates how a single external finding led to unrestricted internal movement because identity barriers were weak. The presenter links rising breach severity to stolen credentials, insider risk, and attackers’ need for identities they can abuse to reach data.

Security budgets still favor network and endpoint tools while identity and defense-in-depth controls receive comparatively little funding. Long, consensus-driven IAM programs, soft-dollar risk benefits, and the myth that identity work is finished after SSO or MFA block progress. The talk describes identity as the remaining perimeter in cloud-era environments and urges an identity-centric operating model that treats customers, partners, and employees with equal rigor.

Practical guidance starts from assuming breach, prioritizing privileged and lateral-movement accounts, and enforcing vetted access with ongoing review. Programs should define identity’s role across the business, rebuild basics in access control and lifecycle management, then integrate identity signals with broader security tooling. Closing Q&A touches vendor collaboration through an industry alliance, parity for external identities, and zero trust as a complement to identity-centric risk decisions.

talks.summary:
The session opens with how email attacks have evolved: socially crafted lures, ransomware aimed at finance and HR, brand and executive impersonation, and security challenges as organizations move mail to the cloud. The first half frames program basics—understanding business risk in messaging, detecting events with threat intelligence and URL sandboxing, applying DLP, reserving related domains, and driving awareness—alongside an integrator and vendor partnership model.

The core presentation maps defenses to the attack kill chain early: ingress policy and antivirus, machine-learned scoring for imposter and malware-free business email fraud, targeted attack protection with sandbox evasion handling, shared intelligence through a central platform, visibility into heavily targeted users, and reanalysis when links weaponize after delivery. It also treats compromised cloud accounts and high-volume internal mail as propagation paths, then covers built-in DLP, outbound encryption, continuity during outages, and automated recall when malicious messages already reached inboxes.

Closing Q&A addresses how fine-grained DLP can be, how threat-response tooling pulls data from other security products without slowing delivery, and how turning on content analysis plus user feedback—and phishing simulation training—improves accuracy over time.

talks.title: Is Your SaaS Secure
talks.teaser: Explains how organizations can secure SaaS applications through visibility, data loss controls and shared responsibility.
talks.summary:
Presented by Optiv with Palo Alto Networks, this webinar looks at how organizations can secure the SaaS applications their staff increasingly use. Nick Mendez of Optiv opens with adoption trends, noting that only about 7% of customers had deployed a CASB for SaaS visibility, while about 24% planned to. He explains the shared responsibility model, in which identity, configuration and data governance fall to the customer, and outlines Optiv's approach of tying cloud security to business goals.

Munem Khan of Palo Alto Networks sorts SaaS use into unsanctioned shadow IT, tolerated apps and sanctioned apps. He gives examples of exposure: a misconfigured AWS S3 bucket that made sensitive records public, files shared to personal email accounts, and a malicious marketplace app that gained account access and was used to phish credentials. He contrasts an inline cloud proxy overlay, which needs log sharing and traffic steering, with using existing next-generation firewalls for visibility and function-level control. For sanctioned apps, he describes the Aperture API service, which scans content for malware and sensitive data and flags risky sharing.

In the Q&A, Nick described one customer that expected 95 to 100 SaaS apps but had close to 200, about half of them unsanctioned. His advice was to discover what is in use, decide what to sanction, and start with an assessment tied to long-term goals.

talks.title: The Six Security Pillars of GDPR Compliance
talks.teaser: Breaks GDPR compliance into six security pillars, covering governance, discovery, classification, access, handling and protection.
talks.summary:
The webinar gives an overview of the GDPR and the six security pillars organizations can use to structure compliance. The regulation covers personal data of people in the EU even when the handling organization sits outside the region, and fines can reach 20 million euros or 4% of annual global turnover. The speakers argue that legal, IT and cybersecurity teams must work together.

Peter Gregory covers each pillar. Data governance keeps management in control of processing, data discovery locates personal data across databases, file shares, cloud services and personal devices, and classification sorts data into sensitivity tiers with handling rules for each use case. Access controls balance convenience for authorized users with blocking everyone else, data handling covers both intended and unintended uses of personal data, and data protection draws on the wider security program. Shawn Ryan then turns to technical controls: anonymization and masking to reduce breach impact and protect non-production environments, database activity monitoring, and tracking of data transfers, while the 72-hour breach notification window is a major challenge that continuous monitoring helps ease.

The closing advice is that compliance is an ongoing change in how an organization operates, affecting legal, IT, security and executive teams. The Q&A covered encryption, which the GDPR does not explicitly require but which should be a defensible, risk-based decision, certification, where no accredited bodies were known at the time, and HR data, which is in scope, particularly with cross-border flows.

talks.title: Endpoint Security Management Creating a Dynamic and Integrated Endpoint and Security Intelligenc
talks.teaser: Shows how unified endpoint discovery, patching, and policy enforcement cut risk when security and IT operations share one view.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why endpoint blind spots and slow patching still dominate breach headlines, using WannaCry and MS17-010 as examples of patches missed long after release. Speakers describe enterprises juggling dozens of point products, security teams that can prioritize but cannot change endpoints, and infrastructure teams that patch without clear risk context. Penetration testing anecdotes—a retailer exposed via vendor VPN and a kiosk path to domain administrator—illustrate how one unpatched or unseen machine can undo broader hardening.

The middle frames three root causes: weak real-time inventory (including roaming devices), inconsistent hygiene, and siloed tools. Recommended capabilities include comprehensive discovery on and off the corporate network, reliable remote patching with high first-pass success, continuous compliance enforcement, and integration so SIEM and incident response see the same endpoint facts operations act on.

The close centers on IBM BigFix modules for patch, compliance, lifecycle, and software inventory, plus relay-based architecture for low-bandwidth endpoints. Integrations with QRadar, Resilience, and third-party EDR vendors are positioned to shorten remediation cycles. Optiv’s role as implementer and managed security provider wraps the pitch: fewer tools, faster minutes-not-hours remediation, and aligned security and operations workflows.

talks.title: Scale Enterprise- Level App Security That Adapts with Your Business
talks.teaser: Shows how to pair automated scanning, programmatic tests, pipeline hardening, and executive dashboards for rapid releases.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing how DevOps shortens release lead times from months to days or less, which turns traditional late-stage security reviews into hard bottlenecks. The first presenter explains why teams that only drop scanners into continuous integration lose the business-logic coverage manual testers provided, and argues that experienced testers should codify recurring checks into automated suites while static and dynamic tools still run in the pipeline.

He extends the scope beyond the application itself to the automation stack—build servers, registries, orchestration, and proxies—because those components hold powerful credentials and can disrupt production if misconfigured. Immutable infrastructure and infrastructure-as-code are praised for scale, but he stresses bringing secure baseline design from operations into developer-owned pipelines. A DevSecOps lifecycle diagram guides discussion of design, infrastructure and container hardening, monitoring visible to engineers, software composition analysis, fuzzing, and centralized triage before findings flood developers.

The second presenter describes IBM’s AppScan family for static, dynamic, mobile, and software composition testing, cognitive reduction of noise, IDE and pipeline hooks, and a modular server-and-client topology. He cites a Forrester-style ROI figure of 253 percent with roughly six-month payback when fully integrated, and walks through a product demo of configured scans, login recording, issue severity views, and reporting. Practitioners should leave with a picture of pairing tool automation, programmatic security tests, pipeline hardening, and executive-friendly risk dashboards.

talks.title: How to Achieve Cyber Resiliency through Efficiency and Automation
talks.teaser: Shows how automated playbooks cut phishing and endpoint alert triage from roughly half an hour to about a minute.
talks.summary:
The webinar opens with a problem the presenters say many enterprises face: a typical organisation runs around 75 security tools, and each one adds alerts that someone must investigate and triage. At the same time, the field faces a large shortfall of cyber security staff. The first presenter argues that automation can take over repetitive enrichment and first-response work, but that automation platforms are complex, that playbooks must be fitted to each environment, and that vendor APIs vary widely in documentation and functionality.

The second presenter described an integrated security fabric approach, built around broad coverage, automated response that removes humans from the first steps, and API calls in both directions to pull in threat intelligence and push actions to other products. The presenters then walked through two use cases. In a phishing alert workflow, the fastest manual run took 26 minutes, while the automated version completed the enrichment, sandboxing and hunt in 1 minute and 29 seconds. In an endpoint alert workflow, a little over 30 minutes of manual work dropped to 59 seconds once automated. Containment steps such as isolating a host or resetting an account were discussed as actions that still need analysis before they are taken.

The closing section argued that cyber resilience depends on continuously validating that controls still work after infrastructure changes, since point-in-time assessments happen only periodically. Practitioners were advised to measure time to detect and time to respond, to design playbooks around their own environment, and to check what an API can really do before relying on it. A short Q&A covered public cloud availability, licensing based on appliance size, and market position.

talks.title: A Radical Approach to Risk Management
talks.teaser: Frames cyber risk through root-cause controls, prevention-first endpoints, and lower-friction programs that cut alert noise.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a Panama Canal history lesson used as a metaphor for cybersecurity. Early French efforts failed because the design ignored local conditions and malaria controls relied on harmful quinine rather than attacking mosquito breeding. After the United States shifted to a lock-based design and a sanitation program grounded in Ronald Ross’s discovery of mosquito transmission, worker death rates fell sharply and the canal was finished in roughly four years. The speakers argue that enterprise security often repeats the same mistake by treating symptoms instead of root causes, which perpetuates what they call the cyber risk cycle and drags on business velocity.

Woodrow Browne draws parallels between malware on endpoints and human-targeted social engineering, citing shared platforms and emotions such as fear and urgency. He critiques endless vendor churn, implicit costs of repeated proof-of-concept swaps, and narrow lab tests that exercise only one slice of the kill chain. Malcolm Harkins outlines a control model spanning prevention, detection, and response across automation levels, adding control friction as a drag on users and processes. He contends many programs remain semi-automated and reactive partly because the security market benefits from unresolved risk.

The closing guidance favors automation, prevention-first tooling, and moving toward lower risk at lower operational cost. Audience questions address layering endpoint detection and response atop strong prevention, rolling out the Silence platform through alert mode toward quarantine, and how multiple heavyweight endpoint agents increase friction, CPU use, and operational complexity.

talks.title: Discussion with SecureAuth and Optiv
talks.teaser: Traces a healthcare payer's federation of four portals with SSO, risk-based auth, self-service registration, and hosted consumer identities.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a narrative about how enterprise access control outgrew the physical data center: virtualization, cloud applications, remote work, contractors, mobile devices, and microservices widened the attack surface while password sprawl and compliance pressure made identity programs harder to govern. The speakers frame identity and access management as a maturity journey spanning identity data quality, joiner-mover-leaver processes, privileged access, adaptive multi-factor authentication and single sign-on, role-based access governance with certification, and protections for unstructured data.

The core case study is a large West Coast healthcare payer refreshing web and mobile channels for members. They faced parallel legacy and new portals, weak prior authentication, low adoption, compliance alignment, and users who might authenticate as employees or as customers. The described deployment added federation and single sign-on across four portals, self-service password reset and intuitive registration, context- and risk-based strong authentication, phased coexistence of old and new portals, and a software-as-a-service user repository that shifted consumer identity liability away from the payer.

A live walkthrough shows first-time MFA with flexible verification channels, reduced friction on trusted repeat access, and blocking anonymized Tor login attempts. Discussion closes on portal threat models—including account takeover, credential stuffing, bot scraping, and synthetic registration fraud—and on aligning security, business, and operations stakeholders so stronger controls still support adoption.

talks.title: The IBM AppScan Family
talks.teaser: Covers DevSecOps bottlenecks, pipeline integration, and how IBM AppScan supports static, dynamic, and correlated app testing.
talks.summary:
The session frames enterprise application security around shortened DevOps lead times and the friction of late-cycle manual assessments. Phil Brass explains why scanner-only shortcuts fall short, how security teams can encode manual expertise into automated test suites, and why Jenkins, source repositories, Kubernetes, and other pipeline software need the same scrutiny as production apps. He also stresses secure infrastructure-as-code, sharing attack telemetry with engineering dashboards, software composition analysis, fuzzing, and centralized triage before findings reach developers.

Much of the middle covers organizational models such as secure design through monitoring, plus Optiv consulting for reference tool deployments, custom pipeline plugins, assessments across web, mobile, API, and cloud targets, and broader SDLC program work. Marlin Machado follows with IBM’s AppScan portfolio: static and dynamic analysis, mobile coverage, machine learning for false positives and fix grouping, flexible licensing, and a topology spanning enterprise servers, automation engines, IDE plugins, and AppScan Standard for professional testers.

A packaged AppScan Standard demo walks through login recording, policy selection, full scan execution, and reviewing data, issues, and remediation tasks. Takeaways for practitioners are to integrate baseline scanning early, preserve high-value manual knowledge as code, secure the delivery toolchain, and present correlated, risk-based posture views to both engineers and management.

talks.title: Identity and Access Management: The Strategic Imperative
talks.teaser: Explains why a strategic, people-and-process-first identity and access management program beats buying isolated tools.
talks.summary:
This Optiv-hosted webcast argues that identity and access management sits underneath most security work and shapes how employees and customers experience an organization. Janelle Jacque, a senior director of strategic consulting, explains that many organizations run it as a collection of disconnected tools. She cites 81% of hacking-related breaches tied to weak or stolen passwords, and says 76% of IT staff have experienced or know of lost or stolen company data. Shared standards for administrative and service account passwords can let one compromised account open the wider environment.

The middle of the talk covers common mistakes, such as buying a product and expecting it to solve problems, deploying tools in an ad-hoc way, and neglecting people and process. The speaker outlines a program view with planning, building and run phases, and breaks the work into identity data, user lifecycle management, authentication, privileged access management, and governance. Governance covers segregation of duties, access reviews and role-based access control, while data classification decides when to require multi-factor or adaptive authentication. Benefits are framed as risk mitigation and business enablement, including audit evidence and faster onboarding.

To close, the speaker recommends starting with a visible early project, such as privileged access vaulting, to build credibility, then offering a centralized service that other business units can adopt. Training and communication across the organization are treated as ongoing work. The main takeaway is that identity programs are complex but achievable when approached in manageable steps under a shared strategy and vision.

talks.title: Salt the Cloud and Make It Rain
talks.teaser: Explains why multi-cloud growth strains security and how automation and shared DevOps culture help bring security into delivery.
talks.summary:
This webinar, presented by an IDC research director and an Optiv automation director, starts from the idea that digital transformation moves applications, users and data outside the network perimeter. The IDC speaker describes the shift from mainframe and client-server computing to a third platform built on cloud, mobile, analytics and social tools, and argues that the castle-and-moat model no longer decides who gets access. Survey figures presented in the talk show security is only embedded in digital initiatives at the most mature 17% of organizations, while most organizations now run in multiple clouds, with only 28% still in a single cloud.

The middle of the session shifts to DevOps as a shared-success culture, where the presenters argue that security must join development and operations early rather than acting as a final stop before release. The Optiv speaker describes how the team builds infrastructure as code, using human-readable files kept under source control, so that network layers, access controls and data lake components can be rebuilt, scaled or moved between providers. Automation handles repetitive deployments, while the last 20% of each environment is customized by hand. He stresses that maintenance usually costs more than initial development, which is why loosely coupled, vendor-agnostic components are preferred. Survey figures on managed services show security is the top application service being managed, at 53%.

The closing discussion covers multi-cloud security and interoperability. The presenters note that every new environment can introduce unreviewed data flows, and that codified infrastructure lets teams redeploy a fixed version quickly to replace a vulnerable one. For cross-cloud consistency, they recommend a platform-agnostic toolset that the organization owns. Practitioners should take away three points: treat infrastructure as software, align teams around shared goals, and automate security checks from the beginning of each project.

talks.title: Find the Poison Needles in the Haystack
talks.teaser: Shows how user behaviour analytics ranks risky users so analysts can spot malicious activity buried in floods of alerts.
talks.summary:
The webinar starts from the problem that security teams are overwhelmed by alerts spread across many separate tools. The speakers describe customers receiving thousands, and sometimes over a hundred thousand, alerts a day, and argue that merging consoles into one SIEM only combines the noise. Their remedy is user and entity behaviour analytics, which builds a baseline for each user and correlates data from sources such as badge readers, email, chat and HR systems to show who needs attention first.

A live demo followed an analytics dashboard that ranks users by risk score. One example user scored 99 against a weekly average of 49. The entity timeline showed a phishing link received around 5 a.m. and downloaded, command-and-control style traffic at 7 a.m., and later VPN login attempts from several countries. The presenter also showed pseudonymised names that are revealed only through a formal HR or legal case, and noted that risk scores update hourly while risk levels change over days.

In the Q&A, the presenters said the product complements rather than replaces a SIEM, is licensed per user rather than per data volume, needs no endpoint agent, and can baseline IoT and industrial devices by their MAC addresses. Deployment can be cloud or on-premises. The main takeaway is that analysts should start with the users whose behaviour departs most from their role and normal baseline, using context about intent to separate noisy anomalies from malicious activity.

talks.title: Defending Healthcare Against Crippling Cyber Attacks
talks.teaser: Explains why healthcare draws ransomware attacks and outlines patching, automation and endpoint defenses that can limit the damage.
talks.summary:
This vendor webinar looks at how healthcare organizations can defend against disruptive cyber attacks. The presenters say a 2018 global threat report ranked healthcare second among the most attacked industries, with smaller clinics and offices often hit because they are easier to breach. Patient identity data was described as more valuable to criminals than card numbers, since it stays useful for years.

The middle of the session covered the threat landscape. The speakers said close to 95 percent of healthcare attacks seen in 2017 involved malware, most of it ransomware. One case described a ransomware attack on a patient-records provider that left about 200,000 doctors unable to reach their data, while an extortion-focused actor was described as threatening to leak stolen records and publicly naming victims. They argued that most malware exploits known vulnerabilities in a few applications, so patch, asset and configuration management come first, and embedded medical devices must be found and segmented. Timing a tier one analyst's endpoint alert triage showed about 30 minutes manually versus under a minute with an orchestration tool.

The closing advice was to get the basics right before advanced tactics, choose tools that are easy to deploy, keep assessing risk, add threat hunting and threat intelligence, and check vendor API documentation before automating. The presenters also described their endpoint agent's prevention, detection and response features and a breach-prevention warranty. The Q&A covered patching in healthcare, the effort behind playbooks, and recovering infected environments.

talks.title: Four Ways Replacing AV with a Security Platform Can Help You
talks.teaser: Explores modern attack trends and how consolidating endpoint controls on one cloud platform can cut complexity.
talks.summary:
The session opens with cheap stolen credentials, passports, voter records, and off-the-shelf remote access tools on public and dark markets, then walks through Carbon Black’s quarterly incident response findings: attack growth by sector (financial, healthcare, retail, manufacturing among leaders), roughly half of investigated intrusions tied to Russia and China, rising counter–incident response behavior, island hopping in about half of cases, and growing IoT targeting. Walt Powell frames the endpoint as the dominant entry path—phishing, credential theft, living off the land, lateral movement, and staged exfiltration—and notes that many breaches begin without traditional malware.

David Gruber argues that stacking dozens of point products raises cost and complexity without matching efficacy, and outlines Carbon Black Predictive Security Cloud as a single-agent, cloud platform combining next-gen antivirus, endpoint detection and response, expert triage, data-center and live query capabilities, and threat hunting. He describes continuous unfiltered endpoint telemetry, streaming behavioral analytics modeled on fraud detection, large-scale cloud processing, software reputation, open APIs, and integrations with common security stacks.

The close ties platform use to stronger prevention (including behavioral blocking offline), earlier visibility in the kill chain, faster investigation and live remediation, simplified deployment, and shared data with orchestration and other tools. Brief Q&A covers PCI compliance with AV replacement, coexistence with existing Carbon Black products, staffing and rollout timelines, and Optiv services for design and managed operation.

talks.title: Threat Intelligence Automation - The Next Step in SOC Evolution
talks.teaser: Shows how blocked endpoint files are sandboxed, linked to related malware and actors, and turned into shareable indicators.
talks.summary:
Optiv and CrowdStrike present a webinar on automating threat intelligence to ease the flood of alerts facing security operations teams. Kurt Baker introduces CrowdStrike's Falcon X, which he presents as a way to automate the creation and delivery of intelligence. He argues that analysts face far more alerts than they can investigate, and cites breakout time, the window before an intruder moves laterally, averaging 1 hour and 58 minutes in the 2018 data he shares.

The demonstration follows a file that an endpoint protection product blocks and quarantines. Falcon X sends the quarantined file to a malware sandbox, produces a risk assessment, and searches a large malware collection, returning six related hashes. The file is attributed to the Goblin Panda actor, and the actor profile lists targeted nations, industries, frequently used vulnerabilities and command-and-control domains. Indicators can be exported and imported into a firewall, and the speaker says the full investigation takes about six to eight minutes. The Premium tier adds intelligence reports, custom malware analysis and API access. In the Q&A, Baker explains why related-malware searches matter because attackers reuse code and infrastructure, and says closed criminal forums matter more than open dark web sites.

Walter Powell then describes Optiv's plan, build and run services for deploying CrowdStrike, and mentions managed EDR services planned for 2019. The main takeaway is to treat quarantined files as evidence, enrich alerts with actor and related-sample context, and measure response against the one-minute detection, ten-minute investigation and one-hour eradication targets the speaker cites.

talks.title: MVISION Cloud - Securing Data from Device to Cloud
talks.teaser: Shows how a cloud access security broker extends data loss prevention and access controls to SaaS, IaaS and unmanaged devices.
talks.summary:
The webinar opens with a short introduction to the partner firm's consulting services, then turns to data security once corporate data lives in cloud services and on personal devices outside the network perimeter. The first presenter argues that classic network controls lose visibility in SaaS, IaaS and PaaS environments, and that a cloud access security broker can extend data loss prevention, governance, access control and threat protection to those services without requiring an endpoint agent.

The middle of the session covers the three control channels: API integrations that act out of band on sanctioned services, reverse proxy checks that classify managed and unmanaged devices during federated login, and forward proxy controls for shadow services. A live demo logs into Office 365 and shows a OneDrive upload containing two or more Social Security numbers being quarantined and replaced with a notice, a file shared from a document to an external Gmail address being blocked, and a download attempt from an unmanaged browser session being stopped while web access stays available. The presenter also described IaaS checks such as storage misconfiguration, provisioning sprawl and malware on workloads.

The closing Q&A compared the approaches. The presenter advised choosing API controls for sanctioned services where possible, reverse proxy for unmanaged devices on federated services, and forward proxy for shadow services on managed devices. The practical takeaway is that no single channel covers every case, so a layered approach is needed to protect data across cloud services and device types.

talks.title: Thomas DeFelice: Fostering a Culture of Security Across the Enterprise
talks.teaser: Offers advice on building security culture through business partnerships, internal champions, and interactive awareness training.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security programs should not be built in isolation. The speaker recommends engaging business partners early, before an initiative reaches production, and framing the work as support for what those partners are already trying to do. He also suggests finding internal champions who act as liaisons and evangelists, and notes that some of his strongest team members came from other disciplines after developing an interest in security.

For awareness, the speaker advises making training interactive, using gamification and healthy internal competition, and tying lessons to personal life, since good security habits at home carry over to work. He describes security as a people, process and technology problem that is increasingly part of business strategy, so risks should be expressed in business terms and folded into enterprise risk management.

For security leaders, the key skills are clear presentation and writing, translating technical issues into ideas a non-specialist can follow, and adjusting the message and data points to the audience, whether that is a board or the wider organization. Becoming more business savvy, understanding partners' concerns and the industry context, lets security show where it enables the business to succeed.

talks.title: ’s Next-Gen SecOps
talks.teaser: Presents a four-pillar framework for maturing SecOps via automation, orchestration, analytics, and reporting.
talks.summary:
The presentation positions modern security operations as a planning, build, and run discipline centered on automation, orchestration, analytics, and reporting. It cites Forrester research that 65% of enterprise security decision makers struggle to hire people with the right skills, alongside evolving attacker techniques, growing event volume, weak SOC prioritization, and fragmented toolchains that slow meaningful response.

The core framework groups work into four areas. Enterprises should adopt stronger prevention and detection controls while avoiding unactionable alert floods. Orchestration, automation, and analytics process high-volume telemetry, free analysts for threat intelligence, and sharpen incident prioritization. Real incidents demand fast hunting for lateral movement, host isolation, and forensics, supported by ticketing workflows. Reporting ties strategy and maturity to threat models, attack-scenario use cases, and KPIs such as time to detect and respond, feeding training and continuous improvement.

The close describes a maturity workshop and assessment, a governance roadmap with defined KPIs, integration of platforms and playbooks with leading orchestration vendors, and outcomes measured by incident volume and mean time to resolution. The intended takeaway for practitioners is that SOC effectiveness depends on measured maturity and integrated automation, not controls alone.

talks.title: Cyber Security Super Heroes: Ben Walcker
talks.teaser: Cyber Security Super Heroes: Ben Walcker.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk profile, Ben discusses his role as a client director at Optive, where he assists organizations in planning, building, and running their cybersecurity programs. He emphasizes taking client security concepts from initial ideas through to daily execution, with the core goal of helping companies stay out of the news regarding breaches and insider threats.

### Key Topics
- **Client Relationship & Program Execution**: Ben details how his work centers on translating strategic security ideas into operational execution to mitigate threats.
- **Overcoming Organizational Silos**: A key focus of the discussion is breaking down fractured relationships within client enterprises, specifically bridging gaps between internal security and networking departments.
- **Team Dynamics and Professional Growth**: Ben highlights the value of working within a multidisciplinary team offering diverse technical and sales backgrounds, as well as leveraging comprehensive advisory, product, and services capabilities.

### Technical Details
Because this presentation is a brief professional spotlight rather than an in-depth technical seminar, specific technical architectures, tools, protocols, or CVEs are not discussed. The primary focus is organizational and consultative: navigating internal friction between security and networking units in a large manufacturing client and assessing the technical makeup of an organization before proposing solutions.

### Takeaways
- Effective cybersecurity delivery often requires addressing organizational culture and internal silos before addressing technology directly.
- Taking an advisory-first conversational approach rather than pitching products immediately builds critical collaboration between divided security and networking teams.
- Having access to full-spectrum offerings—including advisory, product, and services—allows client directors to better understand and solve the real-world operational challenges organizations face.

talks.title: Black Hat 2016 Arsenal Demo: SERPICO
talks.teaser: Demonstrates Serpico, an open-source tool for writing penetration test reports and sharing findings across a team.
talks.summary:
Serpico is presented as a lightweight, open-source report writing and collaboration tool for penetration testers. It is built on Ruby with Sinatra and a few gems, and it runs on small hardware such as a Raspberry Pi, so testers can write reports on site. The demo covers administration: local or LDAP authentication, and two user roles, where administrators can see every report while basic users see their own reports and any they share with colleagues. Reports are based on templates that use a markup language to fill in company names, consultant details, and findings tables automatically.

The presenter then builds a report from start to finish. Client details are entered once, a scoring method such as DREAD is chosen, and findings are added from a shared database, each with its own summary, proof of concept, affected hosts, remediation, references, and screenshots. New findings submitted by users are held for administrator review before they join the shared library. The same data can produce a Word report or a slide deck for a client debrief. The tool can also export a local instance to JSON and import it into a master server, although attachments are not carried over. A newer feature connects to the Metasploit database, pulls in hosts and vulnerabilities, and maps them automatically to finding templates.

The main takeaway is that Serpico is meant to cut the repetitive formatting and copying that slows down assessments, leaving testers more time for analysis. Installers for Debian packages were shown, with a Windows installer still in progress. The project is open source, and feedback, issues, and pull requests are welcome.
